Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Efraim Diveroli's father hoped his son would become a doctor or lawyer. Efraim Diveroli, 22, is doing his "patriotic" duty as an arms dealer, his grandfather says. What he got instead is a 22-year-old international arms dealer who faces a congressional inquiry for allegedly selling old Chinese ammunition to the U.S. military to equip allies in Afghanistan. Diveroli is president of AEY Inc., a South Florida company which, according to U.S. government documents, has done more than $10 million of business with the U.S. government since 2004. The papers also reveal the company struck it big in 2007 with contracts totaling more than $200 million to supply ammunition, assault rifles and other weapons to the Afghan National Army and police. The company's contract said it would get the ammunition from Hungary. But Army investigators found what the Afghan military got included corroded ammunition made in China as long as 46 years ago. The New York Times reported Thursday that AEY shopped stockpiles and ammo dumps in old Soviet bloc allies, from Albania to Kazakhstan. Albania was a big customer for Chinese armaments in the 1960s and '70s, the Times reported. Angelo Diveroli, Efraim's grandfather, told CNN affiliate WPLG-TV that his grandson is being targeted by "jealous competitors" in the international arms market. Since he was a boy, the grandfather said, Efraim Diveroli has known his way around weapons. Read the WPLG story . "He's a genius about anything to do with weapons," the 72-year-old says. "Ever since he was a little boy, I would take him to gun shows and he could identify every model of guns. People would ask: How can he do that so young? He has a gift, I would tell them.'' Michael Diveroli, Efraim's father, told CNN affiliate WFOR-TV that he wished his son had turned his intellect elsewhere. He said Efraim was "a boy genius" who is "hard to control." Read the WFOR story . "I would prefer he became a nice Jewish doctor or lawyer rather than an arms dealer," WFOR quoted Michael Diveroli as saying.  Watch how father says son runs his own show » . But his son seem to have a good idea of the circles he was running in. "What goes on in the Albanian Defense Ministry," the New York Times quoted him as saying. "Who's clean? Who's dirty? Don't want to know about it." On a MySpace page Efraim Diveroli last updated in 2005, he says "I probably grew up way to (sic) fast." But in a hint of where the then-19-year-old's future was heading, he wrote, "I definately (sic) have the desire to be very successful in my business and this does take up alot (sic) of my time." The MySpace page also hints of his need for thrills. "I'm one of those guys who needs to be entertained and having lots of fun all the time so if your (sic) also an undiagnosed case of ADD look me up," it says. He lists the weapon-heavy films "Heat" and "Scarface" among his favorites. A CNN search of Diveroli's Florida criminal record shows arrests, but no convictions, on offenses from misdemeanor battery to felony possession of stolen property. He has yet to appear in court on a March 3 arrest for driving under the influence. For now, relatives say Efraim Diveroli is out of the country. CNN attempts to contact him have not been successful. His grandfather told WPLG that Diveroli is now in Turkey or Albania doing his "patriotic" duty. "He's all over the world getting what the military needs," Angelo Diveroli says. But in a MySpace message exchange with Radar magazine, a person thought to be David Packouz, a 25-year-old who was AEY's vice president, refers to Efraim Diveroli as "my former scumbag partner" and says he is motivated by money. "Efraim Diveroli has a serious psychological illness called 'extreme greed,' " Radar quotes him as writing in a report on its Web site. Packouz would not discuss AEY with CNN on Friday, saying he had no comment "because of the ongoing investigation."  E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Efraim Diveroli’s father once envisioned him pursuing medicine or law. Instead, at 22, Diveroli became an international weapons contractor who, according to his grandfather, was carrying out a “patriotic” responsibility.

Diveroli is the president of AEY Inc., a company based in South Florida. Federal records show that AEY has conducted more than $10 million in business with the U.S. government since 2004. Its business expanded dramatically in 2007, when it received contracts worth more than $200 million to provide ammunition, assault rifles and other arms to Afghanistan’s army and police.

The contract specified that the ammunition would come from Hungary. Army investigators, however, determined that some of the rounds delivered to Afghan forces were corroded, had been manufactured in China and were as much as 46 years old. Diveroli now faces a congressional investigation into allegations that his company supplied the U.S. military with outdated Chinese ammunition intended for American allies in Afghanistan.

The New York Times reported Thursday that AEY searched weapons depots and stockpiles across former Soviet-bloc countries, ranging from Albania to Kazakhstan. According to the newspaper, Albania purchased large quantities of Chinese weapons during the 1960s and 1970s.

Diveroli’s grandfather, Angelo Diveroli, told CNN affiliate WPLG-TV that rival international arms dealers were targeting his grandson out of jealousy. He said Efraim had displayed an unusual knowledge of firearms since childhood.

The 72-year-old described his grandson as exceptionally talented in matters involving weapons. Angelo said he took Efraim to gun shows when he was young, where the boy could recognize every firearm model. When others wondered how someone so young could know so much, Angelo said he explained that his grandson had a natural gift.

Efraim’s father, Michael Diveroli, told CNN affiliate WFOR-TV that he would have preferred his son to apply his intelligence to another profession. Michael characterized Efraim as a difficult-to-manage “boy genius” and said he wished his son had become a “nice Jewish doctor or lawyer” rather than entering the arms trade.

Efraim, however, appeared aware of the environment in which he was operating. The New York Times quoted him discussing Albania’s Defense Ministry and saying he did not want to learn who there was honest and who was corrupt.

On a MySpace profile last updated in 2005, Diveroli wrote—with several spelling errors—that he had probably matured too quickly. At 19, he also expressed a strong ambition to succeed in business and acknowledged that work consumed much of his time.

The profile suggested that he also craved excitement. He invited others who, like him, might have an undiagnosed case of attention deficit disorder to contact him, saying he constantly needed entertainment and fun. His listed favorite movies included the weapons-heavy films “Heat” and “Scarface.”

A CNN review of Diveroli’s Florida criminal history found arrests—but no convictions—on charges ranging from misdemeanor battery to felony possession of stolen property. He had not yet gone to court over a March 3 arrest for driving under the influence.

Relatives said Diveroli was outside the United States, and CNN’s efforts to reach him were unsuccessful. Angelo Diveroli told WPLG that his grandson was in either Turkey or Albania performing what he called his “patriotic” duty. According to Angelo, Efraim traveled around the world obtaining whatever supplies the military required.

A sharply different description came in a MySpace exchange with Radar magazine. A person believed to be David Packouz, 25, who had served as AEY’s vice president, called Diveroli his “former scumbag partner” and claimed money was his primary motivation. Radar reported on its website that Packouz described Diveroli as suffering from a serious psychological condition he called “extreme greed.”

When CNN contacted Packouz on Friday, he declined to talk about AEY, citing the continuing investigation.

Efraim Diveroli, a 22-year-old arms dealer, faced a congressional inquiry amid allegations that his company, AEY Inc., had supplied aging Chinese ammunition to U.S.-backed forces in Afghanistan. Since 2004, the company had conducted more than $10 million in business with the U.S. government. In 2007 alone, it secured weapons contracts valued at more than $200 million.

The controversy centered on an AEY contract that specified ammunition from Hungary. Army investigators, however, reportedly discovered corroded Chinese ammunition that was as much as 46 years old. The findings raised serious questions about the quality and origin of the supplies, as well as AEY’s compliance with its contractual obligations.

Diveroli’s family offered contrasting perspectives on his rapid rise in the arms trade. His grandfather defended him as a knowledgeable weapons expert who was fulfilling a patriotic duty, arguing that jealous competitors were behind the accusations. Diveroli’s father, meanwhile, described him as a difficult-to-control “boy genius.” Although he acknowledged his son’s abilities, he said he wished Diveroli had pursued a more conventional profession, such as medicine or law, rather than becoming an arms dealer.
outputs.L4:
A congressional inquiry and a U.S. Army investigation examined whether AEY Inc., a small Florida-based arms company led by 22-year-old Efraim Diveroli, had violated the terms of a major ammunition-supply contract for Afghanistan. AEY had been hired to provide ammunition to the Afghan army and police, with contracts valued at more than $200 million. The company represented that it would obtain ammunition from approved sources, including Hungary, but investigators found that much of the material instead came from aging Soviet-bloc stockpiles in Albania.

The shipments included Chinese-manufactured ammunition, despite contract restrictions on the acquisition of Chinese military equipment. Evidence indicated that identifying marks had been removed or concealed and that the ammunition had been repackaged before being sent to Afghanistan. Some rounds were as much as 46 years old, and inspectors found cartridges and packaging showing corrosion, deterioration, and other signs of poor storage.

The findings raised questions about whether the ammunition was safe and reliable enough for Afghan security forces fighting alongside the United States. They also exposed weaknesses in the Pentagon’s contracting and oversight systems, particularly the decision to entrust a strategically important supply operation to a young and relatively inexperienced dealer without sufficient scrutiny of his company’s sources and quality-control practices.

Lawmakers sought to determine how AEY obtained the contracts, whether government officials adequately verified the origin and condition of the ammunition, and why warning signs were not addressed earlier. The controversy became a prominent example of the risks associated with wartime procurement, showing how limited oversight and reliance on private contractors could result in U.S. allies receiving old, potentially defective weapons supplies.

### Efraim Diveroli and the Arms-Deal Scandal

Efraim Diveroli is a former American arms dealer best known for securing a major U.S. government contract through his company, AEY Inc. In 2007, the firm received a contract worth nearly $300 million to supply ammunition to Afghan security forces.

The deal later became the subject of federal investigations and widespread media coverage, including reports by major news organizations such as CNN. Authorities discovered that AEY had supplied decades-old Chinese ammunition that had been repackaged to conceal its origin, violating the terms of the contract and U.S. restrictions.

Diveroli pleaded guilty to conspiracy and was sentenced to four years in federal prison. His dramatic rise and fall inspired the 2016 film *War Dogs*, which introduced a wider audience to the controversial world of international defense contracting.
